# How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses

First listed: 2026-09-16 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-bank-stocks-part-1) - 2026-09-16

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman builds bank analysis from accounting, leverage, capital rules and credit provisioning, then argues current bank credit is stable while private-credit warnings may appear elsewhere first. His leverage arithmetic and core CECL timing are useful. The audit corrects the deposit-multiplier framing, exclusive reliance on risk-weighted regulation, rating-agency delegation, Tarullo title/date and CECL history. Some absolute statements confuse uncertain estimates with necessarily wrong accounting, and conditional identities with real-world causation. Current stability does not settle future private-credit risk.

The strongest material is explicit leverage and loss arithmetic, with assumptions retained. Historical and regulatory simplifications require substantial correction. Neither accounting changes nor later stock appreciation prove management motive or a guaranteed contrarian investment outcome.

<a id="substack-213481428-c002"></a>
### 002. An initial deposited dollar is repeatedly lent and redeposited, creating a multiplier of money that powers the economy.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 3:05-4:37](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-bank-stocks-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Bank lending does create deposits, but the fixed initial-deposit multiplier reverses the operational sequence emphasized by the central bank explanation.

Assessment test: Trace the accounting of loan origination, deposits, settlement and constraints.

- [Money creation in the modern economy](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/quarterly-bulletin/2014/q1/money-creation-in-the-modern-economy) (2014-03-14): Commercial-bank lending creates matching deposits; banks do not simply multiply a fixed initial quantity of deposited money.

### 004. Citi has become a successful bank and attractive investment after years of mediocrity.

<a id="substack-213481428-c013"></a>
### 013. With $1 billion equity and $1 billion assets, simple assets/equity leverage is 1 times; deposits would be debt owed to customers.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | supporting

[Source at 11:44-13:59](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-bank-stocks-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

With zero liabilities, assets equal equity and A/E = 1; a repayable deposit is a liability under the assumed contract.

Qualification: Hypotheticals hold after-funding-cost ROA fixed. They do not prove real borrowing leaves ROA unchanged.

Conditional reasoning: With zero liabilities, assets equal equity and A/E = 1; a repayable deposit is a liability under the assumed contract.

Assessment test: Apply assets=liabilities+equity and the stated leverage definition.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary evidence change.

## Framework and tools

- Read accounting as a test of the business narrative.
- Separate return on assets from leverage-driven return on equity.
- Stress loss absorption using capital and asset exposure.
- Compare risk weights with actual underwriting changes.
- Separate loan growth provisions from deterioration provisions.
- Watch credit recognition lags and indicators outside bank statements.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Hypothetical $1 billion-equity banks at 1,10 and 100 times leverage
- ROA and ROE identity
- Risk-weighted versus unweighted capital ratios
- Large-bank CET1 table from Q4 2024 to Q2 2026
- JPMorgan 2020 quarterly credit provisions
- Major-bank nonaccrual table across Q2 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026
- Chip depreciation-life comparison
